title: Moving On

jokes.text: Andy's increasingly tortured logic defending himself: 'And all was good in Scranton, P.A., that day.' / 'Oscar says hi all the time. He says all kinds of greetings — hi, hello, hola.'
jokes.setup: David Wallace confronts Andy about lying — saying 'all is good' while secretly sailing and 'Oscar says hi' when Oscar wasn't there.
jokes.punchline: Andy splits hairs with lawyerly absurdity: the statement was technically true that day, and Oscar does say hi in multiple languages, so the lie stands.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Andy — the narcissist who can't admit fault and finds absurd technicalities to defend himself. The escalation from 'all was good that day' to a multilingual defense of Oscar's greetings is genuinely funny because it reveals Andy's complete lack of self-awareness while being internally consistent with his character.

jokes.text: Andy in confessional listing his problems including: 'I really miss my beard. It was like a security blanket.'
jokes.setup: Andy is listing genuine hardships — losing Erin, losing his 'aha' moments from the boat — building to something emotionally real.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to missing his beard as a comparable loss, delivered with equal sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Works because Andy's self-absorption makes the beard loss a legitimate emotional grievance in his mind. The placement after the real problems and the security blanket simile elevates it from a cheap gag to a revealing character moment.

jokes.text: Andy reciting Bon Jovi lyrics as a poem: 'These five words I swear to you / When you breathe, I want to be the air for you / I'll be there for you. That's a poem by J.B. Jovi. I want you to have it. We are even now.'
jokes.setup: Andy is attempting a grand, heartfelt gesture to thank David Wallace for not firing him.
jokes.punchline: He recites Bon Jovi lyrics as if they were his own poem, credits 'J.B. Jovi,' and declares them 'even now' — as if bad song lyrics are currency.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'J.B. Jovi' is a perfect detail — Andy knows it's Bon Jovi but the formal initial treatment makes it sound literary. The layered absurdity (misattributing, gifting, declaring debts settled with a pop lyric) is pure Andy and could only come from this character. The economy is excellent — the whole bit lands in four lines. Easily quotable and earns its laughs through character specificity rather than randomness.

jokes.text: David Wallace, after Andy leaves: 'Vanilla Ice. He was a band.'
jokes.setup: Andy ends his appeal with 'crystal... vanilla' — an accidental Vanilla Ice reference — and exits triumphantly. David is left alone.
jokes.punchline: David quietly, flatly corrects the implicit misremembering: Vanilla Ice was not a band. Delivered to no one, as a private observation.
jokes.explanation: Four words. Maximum compression. The comedy comes from David's exhausted, low-key processing of Andy's chaos — he doesn't address the insanity of the J.B. Jovi poem, he just quietly fact-checks a minor pop-culture error. The wrongness of 'he was a band' (Vanilla Ice was a solo artist) adds another layer — Wallace himself is slightly off. Excellent economy score.

jokes.text: Andy cheerfully greets Erin 'Good morning. And how are you on this fine d—' then immediately breaks down weeping mid-sentence.
jokes.setup: Andy approaches Erin's desk with a forced cheerful greeting after their break-up.
jokes.punchline: He cannot even finish the sentence before dissolving into sobs, cutting hard from performative okay-ness to total collapse.
jokes.explanation: The mid-word collapse is a structurally clean comedic beat — the setup is Andy trying to hold it together and the punchline is the instantaneous failure. The transcript timestamp gap [02:25] to [02:31] suggests the weeping is sustained and physical, amplifying the cringe. Works because it's earned through the episode's premise.

jokes.text: Andy in confessional, composing himself after crying, then: 'Don't use that part.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just broken down in front of the documentary camera in the confessional.
jokes.punchline: He asks the crew not to use the footage — a classic mockumentary meta-beat that acknowledges his vanity while the audience knows it will absolutely be used.
jokes.explanation: A well-worn Office device but executed cleanly. Works because Andy's concern for his image coexists with his total lack of control. Not especially original — the show has done this beat before — but functional.

jokes.text: Cut to Andy at his desk moaning and wailing like a wounded animal, audible throughout the office.
jokes.setup: Andy's confessional about how hard it is to see Erin every day after the break-up.
jokes.punchline: The moaning and wailing heard through the office — described by a co-worker as sounding like a wounded animal.
jokes.explanation: Broad physical comedy that works in the moment through sheer commitment. The 'wounded animal' line from a co-worker sharpens it. Not subtle, but effective as escalating cringe.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'He sounds like a wounded animal. Should have put him out of his misery and just fired him.'
jokes.setup: Andy is audibly sobbing throughout the office over his break-up.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's solution is mercy-firing — treating emotional distress like an injured farm animal.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Dwight — the farmer's logic applied to the office. Only Dwight would frame firing someone as a compassionate act equivalent to putting down an animal. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'I can't be around sad people. It makes me sad. I'm the same way with horny people.'
jokes.setup: Office workers are commiserating about Andy's sadness being contagious.
jokes.punchline: Meredith equates emotional contagion with sadness AND horniness, delivered as if this is completely normal and equivalent.
jokes.explanation: A gem. Meredith's casual equivalence between sadness and horniness as equally contagious emotional states is perfectly in character — only she would say this. The structure is tight: the sad/sad setup leads you to expect a mirror, and 'horny people' is the perfect Meredith-specific subversion. Highly quotable and character-specific to a degree that approaches the anchor examples.

jokes.text: Erin confessional: 'And hot for us. I mean, I saw Pete's butt. It's sick.'
jokes.setup: Erin explains that she and Pete kept their relationship secret to be considerate to Andy.
jokes.punchline: She adds 'and hot for us' — the secrecy was also titillating — then pivots to a glowing review of Pete's butt with the word 'sick' as superlative praise.
jokes.explanation: Erin's guileless candor — pivoting from consideration to horniness without registering the shift — is true to her character. 'It's sick' as enthusiastic praise is very Erin. Functional and charming but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Pam's confessional: 'It's with a real estate company, which is a great fit for me, because I live in a house and I know what a bathroom is.'
jokes.setup: Pam is describing a job interview Jim set up for her at a real estate company.
jokes.punchline: Her qualifications: she lives in a house and knows what a bathroom is.
jokes.explanation: The self-deprecating logic is well-constructed — the premise (real estate = good fit) sets up a credentials reveal, and the credentials are hilariously minimal. 'I know what a bathroom is' lands with the rhythm of a stand-up punchline. The second qualification is the better of the two, which is the correct ordering.

jokes.text: Pam: 'my resume can fit on a post-it note.'
jokes.setup: Pam admits she's nervous about the interview because it's moving fast.
jokes.punchline: The specific image of a resume that fits on a Post-it note — not just thin, but Post-it-sized.
jokes.explanation: The Post-it specificity elevates a generic self-deprecation joke. Economical and relatable. Complements joke #11 in a nice escalating pair.

jokes.text: Dwight startles Angela at the vending machine and reveals he's been waiting 45 minutes for her in the bathroom.
jokes.setup: Dwight needs Angela's help and has been lurking to intercept her.
jokes.punchline: He was waiting in the bathroom for 45 minutes — the extreme nature of his stalking is revealed casually.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's complete disregard for normal social behavior (lurking in the bathroom for 45 minutes) is in character. The deadpan delivery of an extremely weird fact is a reliable Dwight beat.

jokes.text: Dwight describing Aunt Shirley: 'Her hair, her clothes, it's all falling off in great, big clumps.' / 'We had a nurse, but she quit because she was poisoned by aunt Shirley.' / 'Probably nothing. Or strychnine. Or lemonade and strychnine, which is actually what it was.'
jokes.setup: Dwight asks Angela to help care for his dying aunt Shirley, describing her condition.
jokes.punchline: The escalating revelation: nurse quit → was poisoned → probably strychnine → lemonade AND strychnine → confirmed. Each beat is worse than the last.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation structure. The joke progresses in three distinct beats — each a new reveal that recontextualizes the last. 'Probably nothing. Or strychnine.' is the key pivot, and 'lemonade and strychnine, which is actually what it was' is the perfect closer — the qualification 'lemonade and' makes it more specific and more absurd, and 'which is actually what it was' confirms it with Dwight's signature factual flatness. This is the Schrute family at their best: violence and farming logic applied to human care.

jokes.text: Dwight describing Aunt Shirley's body: 'There's this one hanging part in particular that's some sort of flap. It's like a prehensile wing or something. I don't know.' / 'There's a divot where it was, and it needs—it needs...'
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to convince Angela to help bathe Aunt Shirley by describing what needs attention.
jokes.punchline: His clinical, agricultural description of elderly body parts — 'prehensile wing,' 'divot' — and his inability to name the body part horrifies Angela into agreement.
jokes.explanation: 'Prehensile wing' is a fantastic word choice — it suggests something between an animal feature and a medical anomaly, which is exactly where Dwight's brain lives. The cringe compounds as he keeps going. Angela's horrified capitulation is the correct reaction and mirrors the audience.

jokes.text: Erin to Andy when he questions her leaving early: 'Not on a three-month boat trip.'
jokes.setup: Andy confronts Erin about leaving the office.
jokes.punchline: Erin's immediate comeback references Andy's own months-long abandonment of the office — a callback to his boat trip.
jokes.explanation: Four words that completely shut down Andy's moral authority. The economy is near-perfect — she doesn't need to explain, and the writers trust the audience. The co-worker's 'Oh, burn. Ha.' reaction beat confirms it lands in-universe. Unusually sharp for Erin, which makes it even better.

jokes.text: Andy to Erin: 'Are they from you?' (about messages) / 'Well, then I don't want them.' / 'You can keep 'em. In fact, you can keep that big blue Nautica sweater.'
jokes.setup: Erin tries to give Andy client messages.
jokes.punchline: Andy pivots from refusing work messages to re-gifting Erin his blue sweater — conflating professional duties with the emotional fallout of their break-up.
jokes.explanation: Sets up the blue sweater as an emotional object — important for later payoffs. The 'are they from you?' line is a nice character beat showing Andy's complete inability to function professionally post-break-up.

jokes.text: Erin tells Andy she gave the blue sweater to the Salvation Army. Andy's reaction: 'She got rid of it. My blue sweater. What is that about?'
jokes.setup: Andy gave Erin the sweater as a break-up grand gesture; she donates it immediately.
jokes.punchline: The sweater is gone — Erin has moved on so thoroughly she donated his favorite sweater without hesitation. Andy is devastated by this signal.
jokes.explanation: The sweater becomes a running comedic and emotional throughline for Andy's grief. The gap between how much Andy cares (obsessively) and how little Erin does (donated immediately) is the joke. Good cringe setup for later escalation.

jokes.text: Andy's bro-council: 'We are in the brozone layer. Okay, Nard Dog, Plop, and Clarker Posey, A.K.A. Clarkwork Orange.'
jokes.setup: Andy convenes the male office workers to discuss his emotional situation.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate nicknames ('Clarker Posey,' 'Clarkwork Orange,' 'brozone layer') reveal Andy's juvenile coping mechanism — he's built an imaginary bro-tribe.
jokes.explanation: 'Brozone layer' is a solid portmanteau; 'Clarkwork Orange' is a decent pun. The comedy here is Andy's performative bro-bonding in the face of genuine heartbreak — the gap between the emotional need and the frat-house framing.

jokes.text: Andy asks for advice: Clark says 'Being a bachelor isn't all bad — last night I ordered a pizza by myself and I ate it over the sink like a rat.' Andy: 'There you go. Good for you.' / 'No.'
jokes.setup: Clark tries to spin bachelorhood as liberating.
jokes.punchline: The specific, vivid image of eating pizza over a sink 'like a rat' undermines his argument before he's finished making it. Andy's 'There you go. Good for you. No.' captures the immediate pivot from false encouragement to honest rejection.
jokes.explanation: 'Like a rat' is the key word — the self-awareness of the description makes Clark both the joke-teller and the butt. Andy's 'There you go. Good for you. No.' is a three-beat reaction that earns a laugh at each step. The comedy comes from the intended advice actively making things worse.

jokes.text: Andy, after everyone leaves: offering $100 to whoever will wear the blue sweater to work tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Andy is devastated by the sweater's loss and spiraling.
jokes.punchline: He offers cash to recreate the sweater's presence — the object has become a proxy for the relationship.
jokes.explanation: Extends the sweater running gag and reveals the depth of Andy's dysfunction. The $100 offer is absurdly specific and pitiful in equal measure.

jokes.text: Aunt Shirley to Angela: 'Who's this little kitchen witch? She's so tiny, like a little kitchen witch.'
jokes.setup: Dwight introduces Angela to Aunt Shirley.
jokes.punchline: Shirley fixates on Angela's size with the specific, archaic insult 'kitchen witch' — twice — with the satisfaction of having nailed it.
jokes.explanation: 'Kitchen witch' is a wonderfully specific and unexpected insult — it's the word choice of an elderly Pennsylvanian woman who's been saying the same things for 80 years. The repetition ('she's so tiny, like a little kitchen witch') doubles down as if she's delighted by her own observation. Character-specific and original.

jokes.text: Dwight to Aunt Shirley: 'Angela's gonna get you cleaned up a little bit. Yes. How would you like a nice, warm bath?' / Aunt Shirley: 'How would you like a mean, cold slap?' [Slap sound]
jokes.setup: Dwight offers Aunt Shirley a nice warm bath in a coaxing, gentle tone.
jokes.punchline: Shirley counters the warmth/nice framing exactly: a MEAN, COLD slap — then delivers it.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke construction. The antithetical mirroring — nice/mean, warm/cold, bath/slap — shows a writer who understood the geometry of the setup. The follow-through (she actually does it) makes it physical and immediate. Aunt Shirley is established as a comic powerhouse in one line. This is among the episode's best-crafted individual jokes.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Can I get you a nice crisp liter of schnapps?' Angela objects. Dwight: 'Trust me. It keeps her docile. Go to the kitchen, get the largest receptacle you can find. Step on it.'
jokes.setup: Angela is struggling to manage Aunt Shirley.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's solution is a literal liter of schnapps, casually described as a sedation method, and he asks for 'the largest receptacle' with the urgency of a field medic.
jokes.explanation: 'It keeps her docile' and 'largest receptacle you can find' are perfectly Dwight — the agricultural management of a person. The urgency of 'step on it' applied to fetching schnapps escalates it effectively.

jokes.text: Pete's talking-head: 'It just occurred to me that Andy has been calling me Plop for so long he forgot my real name. Which is Pete.'
jokes.setup: Andy just asked the room if anyone knows a 'Pete.'
jokes.punchline: Pete's quiet, dawning realization — delivered to camera — that his boss genuinely forgot his name because of a demeaning nickname.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to joke #26. 'Which is Pete' — with that period — is the exact right way to end this thought. The understated talking-head delivery makes it hit harder than any reaction shot could. The word 'occurred' implies this is a fresh realization for Pete too, adding another layer. Complementary to #26 and nearly as strong.

jokes.text: Pam at the Philly job interview — her interviewer is clearly a Michael Scott-type, doing voices, saying 'chillax,' whistling. Pam's internal realization: 'Oh my God. He's Michael Scott.'
jokes.setup: Pam is nervous but hopeful about a professional opportunity outside Dunder Mifflin.
jokes.punchline: The interviewer reveals himself to be a Michael Scott clone — the absurdity that you can escape the office but not the type of person who runs it.
jokes.explanation: A structural joke that builds across several minutes. Each escalating Michael Scott-ism (Gangnam Style, Marky Mark, cawfee talk, Kids in the Hall, Bob Dylan impression) sets up Pam's eventual 'Oh my God. He's Michael Scott.' The callback to the original series' most iconic character through a stranger is both a crowd-pleaser and thematically resonant — Pam can't escape this archetype.

jokes.text: Dwight re Aunt Shirley: 'In her prime, Shirls could put away homemade schnapps morning, noon, and night. Now all it takes is 1/2 liter. She's dreaming.'
jokes.setup: Aunt Shirley has passed out quickly after drinking.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's nostalgic lament for his aunt's former drinking capacity — and his slight disappointment in her decline — is a dark reversal of the typical worried-relative dynamic.
jokes.explanation: The elegiac tone Dwight uses to mourn his aunt's drinking capacity is perfectly wrong and very funny. 'In her prime, Shirls could put away homemade schnapps morning, noon, and night' as a fond memory is dark excellence.

jokes.text: Andy reveals to Pete (unknowingly) that he thinks he has chlamydia from Erin. 'I just got off the phone with my doctor, and turns out I contracted ch-lamydia from Erin. And it's incurable.'
jokes.setup: Andy has called Pete into his office to 'get something off his chest' about weird news.
jokes.punchline: The 'weird news' is a fake STI reveal — Andy is manufacturing a scene, except Pete doesn't know this. 'It's incurable' added as an afterthought. 'Pretty lame, huh?'
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is good — the audience (and Pete) expect a professional conversation; Andy delivers a fake STI diagnosis with casual gravity. 'And it's incurable. Pretty lame, huh?' is perfectly calibrated Andy obliviousness. The stunt works because Andy genuinely thinks this gambit will reveal Pete's guilt.

jokes.text: Andy fires Pete by singing a parody of 'Bad Day' by Daniel Powter: '♪ So you had a bad day / The camera don't lie / You're a big idiot, get out of my office / Turns out you're fired because you suck / And you're fired'
jokes.setup: Andy just found out Pete is dating Erin and declares he's firing him.
jokes.punchline: Rather than fire him with any authority, Andy improvises a song to the tune of 'Bad Day' with amateur lyrics, then continues scatting as he leaves.
jokes.explanation: Andy-as-singer-in-crisis is a perfect character beat — his impulse to process emotions through performance is his defining trait. The song is intentionally bad ('You're a big idiot' rhymed with nothing, 'because you suck' as a lyric) which is the joke. Only Andy Bernard would fire someone through an improvised pop song.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Nellie was a professional grudge. This is a purely personal grudge.'
jokes.setup: HR is reminding Andy he can't fire people over grudges, citing the Nellie situation.
jokes.punchline: Andy reframes it: Nellie was a professional grudge (legitimate), Pete is a personal one — as if there's a meaningful legal distinction.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharper Andy lines in the episode. The construction is elegant — he accepts the premise that grudge-firing is wrong but attempts to introduce a taxonomy of grudges that exempts his. The word 'professional' used to mean 'more legitimate' when describing a grudge is a perfect inversion. Economy is excellent — this is a complex logical maneuver compressed into one sentence.

jokes.text: Andy reading the relationship disclosure contract: 'Every phrase is like a dagger in my crotch.'
jokes.setup: HR presents Andy with the relationship disclosure form that Pete and Erin have already signed.
jokes.punchline: Andy describes reading boilerplate HR language as experiencing genital stabbing — the melodrama of his emotional state finding a new anatomical metaphor.
jokes.explanation: The metaphor is unexpectedly anatomically specific in a way that earns a laugh — 'crotch' is the right word choice over a more polite alternative. Andy's tendency to externalize emotional pain in physical terms is consistent with his character.

jokes.text: Andy tears up the relationship disclosure form. HR: 'Andy, that's not the original. And destroying it will not stop them from dating.'
jokes.setup: Andy dramatically rips up the form to assert power over the situation.
jokes.punchline: It's not the original. And even if it were, it wouldn't matter.
jokes.explanation: The double deflation — wrong document AND meaningless gesture — is efficient comedy. The dry HR follow-up has a Michael-era energy. The pause after then confirmation 'It's the original' is a nice timing beat in the transcript.

jokes.text: 'It's the original.' (beat after Andy destroys it)
jokes.setup: HR said it wasn't the original. Andy destroys it triumphantly.
jokes.punchline: It was the original. Delivered flat, after the damage is done.
jokes.explanation: Three words, delivered perfectly flat, after the beat. Maximum economy. The timing structure — the lie to dissuade, Andy ignoring it, the quiet correction — is a clean three-act joke in miniature.

jokes.text: Mark the interviewer: 'I'm the horrible boss around here, but please don't hire Jamie Foxx to kill me.' / 'Django' / 'I don't agree with the use of the n-word in that movie. It's too soon.'
jokes.setup: Mark is doing a series of cultural references to seem relatable/fun.
jokes.punchline: He invokes Django Unchained, then immediately opines on its racial language with the absurd temporal judgment 'It's too soon' — as if slavery were a recent event.
jokes.explanation: 'It's too soon' about slavery is a perfect Michael Scott-level oblivious statement — the well-meaning guy who says something that reveals his complete lack of perspective. Cringe comedy working as intended.

jokes.text: Mark: 'They call me Marky Mark around here, because here at Simon Realty we are one funky bunch. Come on, you guys. Raise the roof when I say that. What are you, all temps again today?'
jokes.setup: Mark is trying to project a fun, inclusive workplace culture.
jokes.punchline: Nobody raises the roof; he scolds them for not participating; they appear to be temps he doesn't bother to know.
jokes.explanation: The 'Marky Mark and the Funky Bunch' reference lands as cringe comedy because the employees clearly don't engage, and his frustration reveals the forced nature of the culture. The detail that they might be temps adds an extra layer of workplace dysfunction.

jokes.text: Dwight's farm: the 'private shower area, very tasteful and very rustic' turns out to involve a hose, chains, and a box cutter. Angela refuses to hose Aunt Shirley 'like some animal.' Aunt Shirley: 'Stop your bellyaching and hose me.'
jokes.setup: Dwight promised a 'tasteful and rustic' shower area for bathing Aunt Shirley.
jokes.punchline: The reveal is industrial — hose, chains, box cutter. Angela objects on humanitarian grounds. Shirley overrules her by demanding to be hosed.
jokes.explanation: 'Stop your bellyaching and hose me' is a great line — Shirley has no patience for Angela's squeamishness about a perfectly normal (to Schrutes) bathing method. The joke works because Shirley and Dwight share a worldview that Angela (and the audience) finds horrifying.

jokes.text: Mark the interviewer's self-description of his office: 'This is not so much an office as it is a rec room with a bunch of computers in it. And, frankly, if I had my way, I'd toss the computers in the garbage, but unfortunately we use them for practically everything we do, so... that ain't gonna happen.'
jokes.setup: Mark is showing off the office space to Pam.
jokes.punchline: He acknowledges the rec room vibe, expresses a desire to trash the computers, then immediately recognizes he can't because they're essential — but delivers it as a minor disappointment.
jokes.explanation: The self-awareness of wanting to throw out computers you depend on — and accepting reality with regret — is a specific kind of managerial delusion that feels very Michael Scott. Good character building.

jokes.text: Nellie to Toby about the Scranton Strangler obsession: 'Then what? Another year picking out a stamp? Another six months before you decide to lick it?'
jokes.setup: Toby has been obsessing over the Scranton Strangler case for two years. Nellie tells him to do something — he says he's been drafting a letter.
jokes.punchline: Nellie projects the timeline of his paralysis into the future: a year choosing a stamp, six months deciding to lick it — making his inaction absurdly, specifically quantified.
jokes.explanation: Sharp joke. Nellie's projection of Toby's paralysis into micro-tasks (a year for the stamp, six months to lick it) is excellent specificity — it's not just 'you're slow,' it's a full comedic timeline. The descending scale (year → six months) has good rhythmic structure, and 'lick it' as the final indignity of inaction is a strong closer.

jokes.text: Mark: 'When I say chillax, people chillax. Watch this. Hey, Roger, chillax.' [Beat] Roger: 'No. I heard you.'
jokes.setup: Mark is telling Pam about his leadership presence by demonstrating his 'chillax' command.
jokes.punchline: Roger explicitly confirms he heard and is actively refusing to comply — 'No. I heard you.' — which is a different and more devastating rejection than simply not responding.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. The setup promises a demonstration of authority; the punchline is total authority collapse. But what elevates this above a simple non-compliance joke is Roger's 'No. I heard you.' — he's not ignoring Mark, he's consciously defying him. This implies a workplace where open mutiny is normalized. Economy is exceptional — four words from Roger do everything. A strong candidate for the episode's best joke.

jokes.text: Mark: 'Step this way for the Spanish inquisition. Kids in the Hall. Just — it's not high pressure. It's just a little [Brooklyn accent] cawfee talk. Okay? Like buttah. Come on in here.' [Pam mouths 'Oh my God']
jokes.setup: Mark continues his relentless stream of pop culture references and accents.
jokes.punchline: Three unconnected references in ten seconds (Monty Python, Kids in the Hall, Mike Myers's Coffee Talk) ending in Pam's silent horror.
jokes.explanation: Part of the escalating Michael Scott-alike bit. The rapid-fire cultural refs with no connective tissue and Pam's muted horror is good cringe construction.

jokes.text: Mark does Bob Dylan impression singing Pam's resume back to her, including '♪ Well, I'm kinda cute / and I'm... But I'm married, so... ♪ Leave that be'
jokes.setup: Mark has launched into an extensive Bob Dylan impression as part of the interview.
jokes.punchline: He ad-libs that Pam is 'kinda cute' mid-song, catches himself remembering she's married, and redirects — all while maintaining the Dylan voice.
jokes.explanation: The self-correction within the Dylan voice — 'But I'm married, so... Leave that be' — is the funniest individual moment in the Mark sequence. The attempt to be appropriate while staying in character creates a lovely cringe. It's both inappropriate enough to be uncomfortable and self-aware enough to be funny.

jokes.text: Andy's group confessional: 'You guys were supposed to have my back. Instead, you let a guy named Plop steal my girlfriend.'
jokes.setup: Andy addresses the men who failed to help him
jokes.punchline: He still refers to Pete as 'Plop' while knowing Pete is the one who stole his girlfriend — reinforcing that he never learned Pete's name
jokes.explanation: After the Pete/Plop reveal, Andy still calling him 'Plop' to his face while knowing he's Pete-who-stole-his-girlfriend is a good running gag payoff. The stubbornness of refusing to use Pete's actual name in this context is perfect Andy pettiness.

jokes.text: Darryl defending himself to Andy: 'Hey, boss, I did everything I could. I invited Pete out for drinks. I emailed him shots of my junk.'
jokes.setup: Andy is upset that his friends didn't sabotage Pete's relationship with Erin. Darryl claims he tried.
jokes.punchline: Darryl's escalation from 'invited him out for drinks' to 'emailed him shots of my junk' as equally reasonable deterrent strategies is perfectly absurd.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan commitment to 'emailed him shots of my junk' as a reasonable friendship-sabotage strategy — with zero acknowledgment that it's aberrant — is excellent. The structure of listing it alongside 'drinks' as equivalent options is brilliant economy.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I feel like the guy Juliet dated before Romeo. Probably her boss. And guess what? Juliet's boss also had feelings.'
jokes.setup: Andy is making a literary comparison to justify his feelings.
jokes.punchline: He invents a character ('the guy Juliet dated before Romeo — probably her boss') and then identifies with this invented person's feelings — while also making himself the boss.
jokes.explanation: Andy's Shakespeare revision — inserting a boss character who predates Romeo — is a good absurdist move. The insistence that 'Juliet's boss also had feelings' as a counter-argument to Pete and Erin's suitability is illogical in a specifically Andy way. The self-insert ('probably her boss') goes unnoticed by him.

jokes.text: Kevin, during Andy's self-pitying monologue: 'You got a booger bubble going on there.' Andy: 'Sorry.' Kevin: 'That's okay. My whole life is a booger bubble.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been giving an emotional speech about feeling like Juliet's pre-Romeo boyfriend.
jokes.punchline: Kevin deflates the scene by pointing out a booger bubble, then delivers a devastatingly bleak non-sequitur about his own life.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional joke. The structure is perfect: Kevin interrupts emotional grandeur with the most prosaic possible observation (booger bubble), Andy apologizes, and Kevin's follow-up — 'My whole life is a booger bubble' — pivots from physical comedy to existential despair in five words. It's deeply sad and deeply funny simultaneously. Only Kevin would say this, and only Kevin's specific brand of unknowing pathos makes it land. The economy is outstanding. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Pam's interview: Mark holds her tiny resume up, calls it 'Papa Smurf, come back to the mushroom.'
jokes.setup: Mark is reviewing Pam's admittedly small resume.
jokes.punchline: He holds it up and addresses it as Papa Smurf returning to his mushroom — comparing the small resume to the tiny Smurf cartoon character.
jokes.explanation: A decent visual gag made funnier by the specificity of 'come back to the mushroom.' The Smurfs reference is dated in a way that fits Mark's character. Complements Pam's earlier Post-it joke about her resume size.

jokes.text: Mark reads Pam's resume upside-down, speaking gibberish, then: 'Oh, wait a second. Now I can read it.' / 'Oh, 'cause it was upside-down.'
jokes.setup: Mark is reviewing Pam's resume at the interview.
jokes.punchline: He was reading it upside-down and apparently couldn't tell. He presents the reorientation as a breakthrough.
jokes.explanation: Broad physical comedy but effectively illustrates Mark's incompetence. The 'oh, 'cause it was upside-down' explanation as if it's a new discovery is a nice touch. Not subtle, but consistent with the Michael Scott parody.

jokes.text: Mark: 'But I like this resume, and here's why. It shows that you stick around. You don't jump ship easily like a lot of these people. I mean, they -- they worship me, you know, but do they like me?'
jokes.setup: Mark is trying to spin Pam's thin resume as a positive.
jokes.punchline: He mid-sentence pivots to a deeply personal insecurity about whether his worshipping employees actually like him — to a stranger he just met, mid-interview.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from resume praise to personal vulnerability ('do they like me?') mid-interview mirrors Michael Scott's inability to maintain professional distance. The detail that he makes this confession to someone he just met in a job interview context is well-observed.

jokes.text: Andy to Pete: 'Kind of painful to chat with you, Pete, ever since the ol' one-two punch to my scrotum pole, translation — penis, translation — my manhood.'
jokes.setup: Andy is being passive-aggressive to Pete about the Erin situation.
jokes.punchline: 'Scrotum pole' as a metaphor for emotional injury, then two translations that get progressively less euphemistic (scrotum pole → penis → manhood), ending more abstractly than it began.
jokes.explanation: 'Scrotum pole' is inventive enough to earn points. The escalating translations that somehow end more abstractly ('my manhood') rather than more concrete is a funny structural inversion. Very Andy — he commits to overwrought language for emotional pain.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Great advice. Thank you. You can leave now.' / Pete tries to be earnest. Andy: 'Awesome perspective. Thanks for butting in.'
jokes.setup: Pete is sincerely trying to counsel Andy on moving on from break-ups.
jokes.punchline: Andy deflects each genuine gesture with performative politeness that reads as hostile — 'Great advice. Thank you. You can leave now.'
jokes.explanation: Standard Office passive-aggression. Works because of the tension between Pete's genuine advice-giving and Andy's inability to receive it. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Mark showing Pam to her desk: 'This will be your desk, right up front. Best seat on the roller coaster. You must be this tall to ride this ride. No pregnant women allowed. Are you? I'm not allowed to ask, so...'
jokes.setup: Mark is showing Pam the front desk position she'd be filling.
jokes.punchline: After comparing it to a theme park ride, he asks if she's pregnant — then immediately notes he's not allowed to ask — while still asking.
jokes.explanation: The legal disclaimer delivered while actively committing the violation is a reliable cringe beat. 'I'm not allowed to ask, so...' followed by expectant silence is textbook Michael Scott behavior. Works in the moment.

jokes.text: Pam realizes the 'office manager' position is a receptionist. Mark: 'Yeah. Like a receptionist, but we call you the office manager, because it's less demeaning.'
jokes.setup: Pam asks what 'office manager' means in practice — answer the phone, forward calls, coffee runs.
jokes.punchline: Mark confirms it's a receptionist job but with the title 'office manager' specifically to disguise its demeaning nature.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical observation about corporate title inflation and workplace condescension. The irony of 'it's less demeaning' — acknowledging the role IS demeaning — is perfectly constructed. Also resonates with Pam's arc: she spent ten years as a receptionist and is trying to move past it, only to be offered a 'receptionist but we won't call it that.' Thematically pointed and economically delivered.

jokes.text: Mark, noticing the documentary cameras: 'By the way, how long are these cameras gonna be following you around? Because I think this is pretty cool.' [Whistles] 'Pretty, pretty cool. Larry David, Curb Your Enthusiasm.'
jokes.setup: Mark notices the documentary crew filming Pam's interview.
jokes.punchline: He references 'pretty, pretty cool' — a Larry David/Curb Your Enthusiasm catchphrase — as a meta-commentary on the documentary format, then explicitly names the show.
jokes.explanation: The meta-commentary on the documentary format is in character — of course Mark would be excited about the cameras — but it's a mildly cheap reference joke. Made better by his critique of Curb ('they indulge themselves a little too much') which is both ironic (he is clearly indulging himself) and another Michael Scott mirror.

jokes.text: Pam's confessional: 'I spent ten years as a receptionist to Michael Scott. And I have kids now. And I just — I can't.'
jokes.setup: Pam is explaining why she won't take the receptionist/office manager job.
jokes.punchline: Ten years of Michael Scott + parenthood = hard no. The specificity of the reasoning and the understated 'I just — I can't' as her final word on the matter.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. Only Pam can deliver this — it references her entire arc on the show and gives 'I can't' the weight of genuine character growth. The joke IS the character's journey, compressed into one sentence.

jokes.text: Angela braiding Aunt Shirley's hair. Shirley: 'Ow. The braid is too tight.' Angela: 'Hush. Loose braids reflect a loose character.'
jokes.setup: Angela is tending to Aunt Shirley's hair while Shirley complains about the tightness.
jokes.punchline: Angela's proverb: loose braids = loose character. A window into Angela's rigid, puritanical worldview applied to hairstyling.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Loose braids reflect a loose character' is Angelas philosophy in microcosm — moral judgment extended to hair. It's aphoristic, original, and could only come from Angela. The structure is a perfect proverb parody with the moral inversion (tight = virtuous) built into the meter. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Nearly at anchor-example level for character integration.

jokes.text: Aunt Shirley to Angela: 'I think your hair is much too long for your age, by the way.' Then: 'Thank you, Angela.'
jokes.setup: Angela has just finished Aunt Shirley's hair under protest.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's thank-you is sandwiched between a backhanded comment about Angela's hair — she returns a catty observation, then sweetly thanks her.
jokes.explanation: Aunt Shirley's cattiness toward Angela is funny — she gives as good as she gets. The simultaneity of the insult and the thanks is good timing.

jokes.text: Toby to Nellie before going to the prison: 'I would understand if he felt motivated to hug me. I would understand if a friendship began. How did Bogart put it? [as Bogart] I think this is the start of my first friendship.'
jokes.setup: Toby is describing his expectations for meeting the convicted Scranton Strangler in prison.
jokes.punchline: He imagines a hug and a friendship beginning, then misquotes Casablanca ('the beginning of a beautiful friendship') to apply to himself — calling it his FIRST friendship.
jokes.explanation: 'My first friendship' is devastating Toby comedy — the implication that Toby has no friends and is pinning his hopes on a convicted serial killer is perfectly sad. The Bogart misquote (changed to 'my first friendship' from 'a beautiful friendship') personalizes the classic line in the most tragic possible way. Very Toby.

jokes.text: Erin to the management consultant (Alice, Pete's ex): 'Cute sweater.' Alice: 'Oh, thanks.' Erin: 'Your shoes match. I'm bad at small talk.' Kevin: 'I'm Kevin.'
jokes.setup: Erin introduces herself to Alice (the new consultant) with small talk.
jokes.punchline: She compliments the sweater, then the matching shoes, then preemptively declares she's bad at small talk — all of which is demonstrably true. Kevin's non-sequitur introduction is the capper.
jokes.explanation: Erin's self-awareness about being bad at small talk while demonstrating it is an accurate character beat. 'Your shoes match' is a funny second observation — it's not a compliment, it's just an observation about basic coordination. Kevin's 'I'm Kevin' as a total non-sequitur is a reliable Kevin beat.

jokes.text: Gabe, upon seeing Erin's new boyfriend: 'Hey Erin, look who's back. The birdman.' / 'Hello, beautiful.' / Kevin to Erin about Andy: 'Didn't you two used to do it?' / Andy: 'We absolutely did. Thank you for remembering that.'
jokes.setup: Andy returns to the office from his annex exile.
jokes.punchline: Gabe's cringe greeting ('the birdman'), Kevin's blunt 'didn't you two used to do it?', and Andy's bizarrely gracious response ('thank you for remembering that') form a three-beat sequence.
jokes.explanation: Three characters, each delivering in their own voice. Gabe's romantic longing ('hello, beautiful'), Kevin's bluntness, and Andy's strange pride ('thank you for remembering that') each hit a different comedic note. 'Thank you for remembering that' is the best of the three — Andy treating Kevin's tactless question as a commemoration of his relationship.

jokes.text: Aunt Shirley to Dwight and Angela about being 'just friends': 'That's what Mose said about his lady scarecrow, and look what he did to that poor thing.'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Angela insist they are 'just friends.'
jokes.punchline: Shirley invokes Mose's 'relationship' with a lady scarecrow as cautionary evidence, implying something unspeakable.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional joke. The setup implies something horrible about Mose and the scarecrow that the audience must fill in — the joke is funnier because it's not explicit. 'Look what he did to that poor thing' as a warning about declaring something 'just friends' implies a romantic-to-physical escalation with an inanimate object. Deeply in the Schrute family's worldview. Character-specific and original; one of Aunt Shirley's best moments.

jokes.text: Andy trying to maximize Erin and Pete's discomfort: 'I mean, you got to admit it, this sure is intense. Having to share a workspace with someone you used to get it on with.' / 'Awkward!'
jokes.setup: Andy has engineered a situation where both Pete and Erin are in the same room as their respective exes.
jokes.punchline: Andy narrates the awkwardness he's created as if he's a bystander — 'awkward!' — while being the architect of it.
jokes.explanation: Andy's disingenuous commentary on the situation he engineered has a nice ironic quality. 'Awkward!' as a teenage declaration from a mid-thirties manager is character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Andy to Pete, after Pete has advised him to 'move on': 'Yeah, so life gives you lemons, you just gotta eat 'em, rinds and all. And, if you don't want to eat 'em, your ex-girlfriend will shove them down your throat with the help of her hunky new boyfriend. So that's fun.'
jokes.setup: Andy has pretended to accept Pete's advice about moving on.
jokes.punchline: He reinterprets 'life gives you lemons' with escalating sourness — eating the rind, then having them shoved down your throat by your ex and her new boyfriend.
jokes.explanation: The lemon metaphor extension is well-constructed — eating the rind escalates the unpleasantness before the punchline (throat-stuffing by ex and new boyfriend) subverts the inspirational idiom completely. 'So that's fun' as the closing tag is perfectly deflated. Andy's ability to make any optimistic cliché sound bitter is well-used here.

jokes.text: Pete's ex Alice to Pete: 'You must be pretty horny.' (after describing his post-breakup weight loss/gain)
jokes.setup: Alice is explaining to Pete why Andy called her to be a consultant — Andy told her Pete and Erin broke up.
jokes.punchline: Alice connects Andy telling her about the break-up with Pete's romantic situation: 'You must be pretty horny.' Delivered as a matter-of-fact inference.
jokes.explanation: Works because it's so direct — Alice states what she thinks without filter. But it's not especially well-constructed beyond the bluntness. The economy is good; the originality is low.

jokes.text: Toby, after the Scranton Strangler strangled him in prison: 'Well, the good news is, no more guilty conscience. At least you know he is the strangler. The proof is in the grip. Did they say when the vocal cords would heal?'
jokes.setup: Toby went to the prison to tell the Scranton Strangler he believed him innocent. Toby returns — implied to have been actually strangled.
jokes.punchline: The silver lining: he now knows the guy IS a strangler ('proof is in the grip'). His vocal cords may take weeks to heal. Nellie's matter-of-fact questions.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding payoff to a multi-season runner. 'The proof is in the grip' is a perfect recontextualization of the idiom — Toby's attempt to vindicate a convicted strangler resulted in being strangled, which confirms the conviction. The dark logic is immaculate. Nellie's clinical 'did they say when the vocal cords would heal?' treats his near-death experience as a logistical matter. This is among the episode's best jokes and one of Toby's greatest moments — years of buildup paid off in one dark, perfectly structured beat.

jokes.text: Toby, hoarse-voiced, on the brave act of offering his neck to discover the truth: 'You offered your neck in search of the truth. The proud neck of justice — isn't that the expression?'
jokes.setup: Nellie is attempting to frame Toby's near-strangulation as noble.
jokes.punchline: 'The proud neck of justice — isn't that the expression?' — It is not an expression. Delivered with earnest uncertainty.
jokes.explanation: 'The proud neck of justice' is a wonderfully fake-sounding proverb. Nellie's earnest question 'isn't that the expression?' signals she's not sure she made it up correctly. The comedy comes from treating a nonsense phrase with the seriousness of a real idiom.

jokes.text: Aunt Shirley after Angela braids her hair: 'I feel like a show pony.' Angela: 'And you look like one too. Thank you.' / Shirley: 'Would you like some stew?' / Dwight: 'And I will carve the roast skunk.'
jokes.setup: Angela has transformed Aunt Shirley's appearance through the bath and braid.
jokes.punchline: Angela confirms the show pony comparison as a compliment; Shirley offers stew; Dwight offers to carve 'the roast skunk' — as if roast skunk is a normal dinner offering.
jokes.explanation: Angela accepting the show pony comparison ('and you look like one too, thank you') while intending it as a compliment is delightfully tone-deaf. 'Roast skunk' as a casual dinner meat is very Schrute. The meal-sharing moment has a warm absurdity.

jokes.text: Dwight offers Angela 'the stink sack' from the skunk: 'You don't eat it. It's a toy, like a wishbone. You know, prettiest girl gets the stink sack.'
jokes.setup: After dinner, Dwight offers Angela the stink sack from the roast skunk.
jokes.punchline: It's presented as a coveted honor — 'prettiest girl gets the stink sack' — a Schrute family tradition equivalent to the wishbone, but for a sack of skunk spray.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most original jokes. The reframing of 'stink sack' as a prize ('prettiest girl gets the stink sack') is peak Schrute worldbuilding — the logic is internally consistent, the detail is specific and strange, and Dwight presents it with sincere gallantry. Angela accepting it as a compliment ('thank you') completes the joke. This works because it's not random weirdness; it follows Schrute farm logic with perfect consistency.

jokes.text: Jim surprises Pam in Philly with champagne after she didn't get the job. Jim: 'Are you all right?' Pam: 'Oh, yeah. I'm more than all right. There's just nothing to celebrate.' Jim: 'It's from the part of France that immediately gave up to the Nazis.'
jokes.setup: Jim has opened champagne to celebrate Pam's interview. She tells him she didn't get the job.
jokes.punchline: Jim reframes it as 'consolation champagne' from the part of France that surrendered to the Nazis — making the wine's provenance match the occasion's mood.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of Jim's best ever. The construction is elegant: consolation champagne needs a provenance story, and France-that-surrendered is the perfect historically resonant but absurd solution. It works on multiple levels: it's self-deprecating for the champagne, it's Jim's specific wit applied to a vulnerable moment, and 'from the part of France that immediately gave up' has a beautiful rhythm. The word 'immediately' is load-bearing — it's more specific and more funny than simply 'surrendered.' This is at anchor example level.

jokes.text: Dwight's romantic plea to Angela: 'I'm not talking about some frisky romp in the warehouse. We have wasted too much of our lives ignoring the fact that we belong together. The 80 or 90 years that I have left of this life... I want to spend with you.'
jokes.setup: Dwight makes a sincere romantic declaration to Angela.
jokes.punchline: 'The 80 or 90 years that I have left' — Dwight, who is roughly 40, calculates he will live to 120-130. The grandiosity of his love declaration is inadvertently undermined by his absurd self-assessed life expectancy.
jokes.explanation: The joke is embedded in a sincere moment — Dwight genuinely means this declaration, which makes the life expectancy calculation both more absurd and more touching. Only Dwight would calculate his remaining lifespan mid-proposal and genuinely believe he has 80-90 years left. The comedy doesn't undercut the sincerity; it IS the sincerity. Character-specific and well-structured.

jokes.text: Andy calls a conference room meeting, pretending to care about everyone's day, then reveals: 'Interesting, because Erin and Pete thought it wouldn't be weird at all. Why do you think it was weird, Gabe?'
jokes.setup: Andy calls an ostensibly normal check-in meeting.
jokes.punchline: The entire meeting was a trap to embarrass Erin and Pete by surfacing their exes — Gabe (Erin's ex) and Alice (Pete's ex), whom Andy has secretly hired as a consultant.
jokes.explanation: The structure of Andy's revenge — engineering a meeting of all the exes — is a good comedic premise. The reveal of the gambit is satisfying because it recontextualizes Andy's behavior throughout the episode (hiring Alice, the meeting invitation).

jokes.text: Gabe: 'I still wear Erin's button-downs around the condo sometimes, so it feels to me like we're still in a relationship... a lot of the time.'
jokes.setup: Andy is asking Gabe about his relationship with Erin to embarrass her.
jokes.punchline: Gabe reveals he still wears her clothes — a deeply unsettling detail delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Pure Gabe — his parasocial relationship with Erin, maintained through fabric. The specificity of 'button-downs' and 'around the condo' makes it vivid and deeply uncomfortable. Gabe is one of the show's great cringe characters and this is peak Gabe.

jokes.text: Gabe about Erin: 'She wouldn't even let me say I love you. It was adorable. She'd plug her ears and scream her heart out.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks Gabe if Erin ever told him she loves him.
jokes.punchline: Gabe describes Erin physically screaming to avoid hearing 'I love you' as 'adorable' — a profound misreading of a clear signal.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Gabe calling Erin's obvious rejection response 'adorable' is the perfect encapsulation of his delusional relationship with her. The image of her literally screaming with her ears covered rather than hear 'I love you' is both funny and quietly devastating. His sincerity makes it hit harder.

jokes.text: Andy to Gabe: 'Because every word out of your mouth is like the squawk of an ugly pelican.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is oversharing about his relationship with Erin.
jokes.punchline: Andy's vivid and specific animal insult — 'the squawk of an ugly pelican' — shuts him down.
jokes.explanation: 'Ugly pelican' is a specifically unmagnificent bird to invoke — pelicans are not classically beautiful and the sound of their squawk is indeed unpleasant. The adjective 'ugly' is redundant for a pelican (they're not handsome birds) which makes it funnier. Characteristic Andy flourish.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'I got a tattoo for you.' / Andy: 'I didn't ask you to get that Nike swoosh. Nobody did. You did that for you.' / Gabe: 'Just do it. You were the it that I was just doing.'
jokes.setup: Gabe makes a grand gesture — he got a tattoo for Erin.
jokes.punchline: It's a Nike swoosh. Andy correctly points out it was self-motivated. Gabe's attempted comeback ('You were the it I was just doing') is a tortured Nike slogan twist.
jokes.explanation: Multiple layers: the Nike swoosh as a romantic tattoo is absurd, Andy's 'nobody did, you did that for you' is a sharp deflation, and Gabe's garbled comeback ('you were the it I was just doing') is a genuinely well-constructed bad pun — it actually works as a sentence while being completely ridiculous. The wordplay is intentionally strained, which is the joke.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'What kind of music are you into, Peter?' Pete: 'Uh, I like all kinds of music, Gabe.' Gabe: 'Really? All kinds? So you like songs of hate written by the white knights of the Ku Klux Klan?'
jokes.setup: Gabe is trying to undermine Pete by interrogating his music tastes.
jokes.punchline: From 'all kinds of music' to KKK songs — the most extreme possible interpretation of 'all kinds,' delivered with Gabe's particular brand of formal aggression.
jokes.explanation: The leap from 'all kinds of music' to KKK songs is absurdly large and beautifully constructed. Gabe's pedantic formalism ('songs of hate written by the white knights of...') treats the logical trap as if it's airtight. Erin's immediate 'No!' shows she sees through it. It's a good joke because it captures Gabe's desperate, slightly unhinged jealousy channeled through a formal debate trap.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'He's not a very sophisticated man. I mean, he can't use chopsticks, so do I need to say anything else?'
jokes.setup: Gabe is building a case against Pete's sophistication.
jokes.punchline: Chopstick proficiency as the metric for sophistication — and Gabe presents it as definitive ('do I need to say anything else?').
jokes.explanation: Gabe's snobbishness (he's been to Japan, he uses chopsticks) applied to romantic competition is peak Gabe. The 'do I need to say anything else?' seals it — he genuinely believes chopstick use is dispositive. Pete's attempted comeback ('chopsticks is not the measure of a man') is the correct response to an absurd argument.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'Come back. One night. Give me one night with you.' / 'I have shaved everything.' / 'I am as smooth as a porpoise for you.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is making his final desperate plea to Erin in the middle of the meeting.
jokes.punchline: His romantic offer is 'one night,' supported by the evidence that he has shaved everything, and the selling point is his porpoise-like smoothness.
jokes.explanation: 'I am as smooth as a porpoise for you' is a hall-of-fame Gabe line. The choice of porpoise over dolphin is specifically Gabe — slightly wrong, slightly formal, slightly off. The preparation ('I have shaved everything') combined with the marine mammal comparison creates a perfectly calibrated cringe moment. This is Gabe at his most grotesque and most hilarious simultaneously. High quotability — it's the kind of line people repeat.

jokes.text: Pam describing the Michael Scott interviewer to Jim over dinner: 'He did half the interview as Ace Ventura.'
jokes.setup: Pam is recounting her interview to Jim over dinner in Philadelphia.
jokes.punchline: Half the interview was conducted in Ace Ventura character — stated matter-of-factly as if this is simply what happened.
jokes.explanation: The Ace Ventura detail adds to what the audience didn't see in the interview scene. 'Half the interview' is the right proportion — not all of it, which would be more extreme; half, which means he also did the other half normally. Good deadpan delivery implied by the transcript.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam guessing the poster in the interviewer's office — Austin Powers, Ferris Bueller, Night at the Roxbury — it's The Odd Life of Timothy Green. 'I'm sorry. How did you think I was expected to guess that?'
jokes.setup: Pam is playing a guessing game about what poster the Michael Scott-ish interviewer had on his wall.
jokes.punchline: After three incorrect guesses of iconic comedy films, the answer is The Odd Life of Timothy Green — an obscure family drama. Jim's response ('How did you think I was expected to guess that?') is the correct reaction.
jokes.explanation: The guessing game structure creates expectation for a silly but guessable answer. The Odd Life of Timothy Green is the perfect wrong answer — not a cult classic, not cool, not even knowingly bad, just a sweet family film that a certain kind of earnest man would love unironically. Pam's follow-up ('he must look at it 20 times a day') adds pathos.

jokes.text: Pam/Jim play 'guess the poster on his wall': Austin Powers? Ferris Bueller? 'You're getting colder.' 'Not Night at the Roxbury.' 'The Odd Life of Timothy Green.' 'I'm sorry, how did you think I was expected to guess that?'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to guess what movie poster the interviewer had on his wall.
jokes.punchline: After logical Michael Scott-tier guesses, the answer is 'The Odd Life of Timothy Green' — so random it's impossible to guess, and Pam reports he cries at it 20 times a day.
jokes.explanation: The guessing game structure is perfectly calibrated — the wrong answers are all reasonable, which makes 'The Odd Life of Timothy Green' land as a genuine surprise. 'I'm sorry, how did you think I was expected to guess that?' is a great straight-man response. The detail that he cries at it 20 times a day ('it's right next to his desk') elevates it further.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's dinner: Pam admits she doesn't know if she wants to move to Philly. Jim: 'Huh.' Long silence. Then: 'This is a little out of left field. Is it?' Another pause. 'I just liked our life in Scranton.' / 'And I have started a business in Philadelphia.'
jokes.setup: What has been a sweet, romantic dinner scene suddenly shifts — Pam reveals she may not want this life.
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'Huh.' and the subsequent silences are the comedy — or rather, the anti-comedy that marks the episode's tonal shift. The juxtaposition of the celebratory champagne scene with this revelation.
jokes.explanation: This is less a pure comedy beat and more a tonal shift that uses silence as drama. The awkward silences are structured as discomfort comedy — the audience laughs nervously — but the scene is also genuinely doing emotional work. Scored lower on quotability because the power is in the silence, not the words.

jokes.text: Cold open of a TV show within the show: 'Little did my grandfather know, mahjong would be here to stay. Hobbies of the East continues in a moment.'
jokes.setup: The TV is on in the background during a scene at Schrute Farm.
jokes.punchline: The program playing is 'Hobbies of the East' — a deeply niche documentary about mahjong. The grandfatherly non-revelation ('mahjong would be here to stay') is delivered with the gravity of historical insight.
jokes.explanation: A background gag that rewards attention. 'Hobbies of the East' as a TV series is a funny invention, and 'mahjong would be here to stay' as a profound historical conclusion is nicely absurd. Not essential but a nice background texture joke.

jokes.text: Andy with gravity boots: 'I watch way too many ads online, and I don't do enough sit-ups. So I bought these. Now every time an ad pops up online, I get 30 seconds of ab-blasting. I call it Ads for Abs. Ironically, I learned about the boots from an ad online.'
jokes.setup: Andy is hanging upside-down in the office in gravity boots.
jokes.punchline: The scheme is explained — he turns ads into exercise — and the irony is immediately noted: the boots themselves were an ad. The closed loop of ad-driven behavior.
jokes.explanation: 'Ads for Abs' is a good invention — the portmanteau has the logic of a real wellness scheme. 'Ironically, I learned about the boots from an ad online' is the self-aware kicker that closes the loop perfectly. Andy's unearned confidence in this system is characteristic.

jokes.text: Kevin asks why Andy doesn't just do regular sit-ups. Andy: 'I'll tell you why. Because... The floor... is... disgusting.'
jokes.setup: Kevin's reasonable question about regular sit-ups.
jokes.punchline: After building anticipation with dramatic pauses, the reason is simply that the floor is disgusting — a legitimate but wildly disproportionate reason to buy gravity boots.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the delivery — the dramatic three-part pause ('Because... The floor... is... disgusting.') builds expectation for a profound answer. The mundanity of the actual reason is the punch. The ellipses in the transcript suggest the timing is everything here.

jokes.text: Kevin refusing to help Andy get down from the gravity boots: 'Oh, why don't your famous stomachs help you now?'
jokes.setup: Andy is stuck hanging upside-down in his gravity boots and needs help getting down.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's sarcastic personification of Andy's abs ('your famous stomachs') as if they're a proud asset that has now abandoned him.
jokes.explanation: 'Your famous stomachs' is excellent — the plural 'stomachs' makes it sound like Andy has been boasting about multiple stomachs, and Kevin's sarcasm is the correct response to the gravity boot situation. Very Kevin in its sideways logic.

jokes.text: Andy escalating his helplessness while upside-down: head rush, offering $20 then 'a pizza' to Kevin, 'I'm not going anywhere. I'll be right here.' while clearly stuck.
jokes.setup: Andy is stuck upside-down in the gravity boots with no help coming.
jokes.punchline: His declaration 'I'm not going anywhere. I'll be right here' — as a threat/promise while literally incapacitated — then escalating bribes from $20 to a whole pizza for Kevin specifically.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of being stuck upside-down combined with the verbal comedy of Andy's failed authority ('I'm not going anywhere') is effective broad comedy. The Kevin pizza bribe is a nice specific character beat — Kevin's price is a pizza, not cash.

tmdb_overview: Pam interviews for a job in Philadelphia, but her potential manager reminds her of her former boss, Michael Scott. Dwight acquires the help of Angela in order to give his elderly Aunt Shirley a bath. Meanwhile, Andy attempts to make Pete and Erin feel uncomfortable.
